name: Anti-inflammatory diet

lead: An anti-inflammatory diet emphasises fish, berries, greens, olive oil and nuts while limiting processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugar and red and processed meat. People in appearance communities use it for a less puffy face and fewer breakouts.

The chain is that omega-3s, polyphenols and fibre lower chronic low-grade inflammation, measured by markers such as CRP and IL-6, which followers link to less puffiness and acne. The Mediterranean diet is commonly given as the model. Research examines inflammation markers and diet indices, mostly for heart disease, bowel disease, depression and cognitive health, and no trials were found on facial puffiness or acne.

paras: People fill plates with fish, berries, leafy greens, olive oil and nuts, and cut back on processed foods and sugar. It is run as a long-term eating pattern, and users report on skin and puffiness over weeks to months.
It is a conventional food pattern, and sources advise discussing individual conditions with a clinician.

angle.text: Users eat whole, low-processed foods to lower chronic inflammation, with less facial puffiness and fewer breakouts as the payoff. Research tracks inflammation markers and disease outcomes rather than puffiness or acne directly.

lead: An anti-inflammatory diet is an eating pattern intended to lower chronic low-grade inflammation by emphasising whole foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols and fibre, while limiting processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugars and red and processed meat.[1] The Mediterranean diet is commonly given as a model.[1] In appearance communities it is cited for reducing puffiness and acne.

Research examines inflammation markers and diet indices, mostly for heart disease, bowel disease, depression and cognitive health. No trials were found on facial puffiness or acne with an anti-inflammatory diet as such.
infobox: Fish, berries, leafy greens, olive oil, nuts
Processed food, refined carbohydrate, red meat

paras: Proponents prioritise fatty fish, berries, leafy and cruciferous vegetables, extra-virgin olive oil and nuts, and avoid fried foods, sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates; Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, describes the aim as lowering markers such as CRP and IL-6.[1]

The Wikipedia page on anti-inflammatory substances notes that omega-3 fatty acids have shown inconsistent anti-inflammatory results and that a 2019 meta-analysis found curcumin did not significantly lower circulating inflammatory markers.[2]

A meta-analysis of Dietary Inflammatory Index studies associated more inflammatory diets with cardiovascular risk and mortality, and another with colorectal cancer risk.[3][4] A review of dietary patterns found associations with inflammation biomarkers in adults.[5] A systematic review and meta-analysis examined anti-inflammatory diets and depressive disorders, and another review covered dietary patterns and cognitive health in older adults.[6][7]

In inflammatory bowel disease, a case series and a randomized trial of fecal microbiota transplantation combined with an anti-inflammatory diet in ulcerative colitis reported outcomes, and a review covered nutrition and gut microbiota in IBD.[8][9][10] A study of low arachidonic acid diet with fish oil in rheumatoid arthritis was also published, and a cardiology review addressed dietary strategies for post-prandial glucose, lipids and inflammation.[11][12] No studies on acne or facial puffiness were found.

lore.intro: The diet is discussed as a way to avoid processed foods for less puffiness and acne.

claims.claim: Cutting processed food reduces facial puffiness and acne.
